title: Practical Prompt Hygiene - Scrapbook
content:
Purpose:
Quick personal notebook for repeated heuristics + micro-templates I keep reaching for. Meant to be light, messy, and usable when iterating on prompts for demos or quick evals. Not canonical — just my brain dump so I don’t re-learn the same gotchas.

Top-level heuristics (one-liners):
- Be explicit about format, but give a tolerant parser: 'Return JSON with fields name, summary; if unknown, return null for field and a short reason string.'
- Anchor behavior with a short system preface: one sentence that defines role + constraint.
- Put the critical instruction first and the rationale last. Helps with left-to-right attention.
- Use 2–3 few-shot examples max for ambiguous tasks; more hurts if examples conflict.
- When testing for brittleness, intentionally invert one example (counterexample) to see if model flips.

Prompt hygiene checklist (quick):
- [ ] explicit output schema (types + missing value behavior)
- [ ] max tokens / truncate policy stated
- [ ] edge case example included
- [ ] allowed hallucination level noted (none / mild / permissive)
- [ ] fallback text specified (error object, apology, or default)

Common failure patterns I hit and mitigation notes:
1) 'Polite deflection' — model refuses with too much hedging when the task is simple.
   Mitigation: add 'You may assume content is non-sensitive for this exercise.' or give short permissive guardrails.

2) 'Overformalization' — model outputs verbose prose instead of compact structured bullets.
   Mitigation: provide 1 exemplar of compact output and say 'Use bullets, max 60 chars per bullet.'

3) 'Hallucinated sources' — when asked for citations, model invents sources.
   Mitigation: require 'If you cannot cite, return "no-citation" for the cite field.'

4) 'Sample sparsity flip' — model follows early examples too literally.
   Mitigation: ensure variety in examples and add explicit branching rule: 'If input contains X then do Y else Z.'

Mini-template bank (micro-templates I reuse):
- ROLE-FIRST JSON
System: You are a concise assistant that outputs JSON only.
User: "TASK: summarize product feature as {title, one_line, bullets}. ALWAYS produce valid JSON. If unknown field, use null"

- CLARIFY-OR-ASSUME
User: "If you need missing details, ask one clarifying question. If none can be asked, make a single reasonable assumption and label it in 'assumptions'."

- REDUCE-TO-EXAMPLES (for NER / classification)
Provide 2 few-shot labeled examples + 'Return labels as [A,B,C]'.

Few-shot set (compact) — used for intent classification experiments:
Example 1:
  Input: "How do I reset my password?"
  Label: account_recovery
Example 2:
  Input: "Can I get reports for last quarter?"
  Label: export_reports
Prompt stem: "Label the user's intent among: account_recovery, export_reports, billing_help, general_info. Return a single label string."

Failure-case experiments to run (prioritized):
- Swap order of examples and see if label distribution flips. (Hypothesis: small models are order-sensitive.)
- Add a 'contradictory' negative example that looks similar but maps to a different label.
- Introduce typos and slang — evaluate recall and precision drop.

Example diagnostic session (notes):
- Model: redwood-compat-7B-quant (local sandbox)
- Prompt: ROLE-FIRST JSON + 2-shot intent examples + stem
- Observed: baseline accuracy 0.85 on clean test set, drops to 0.56 with typos; restoring second example with paraphrase improves to 0.70.
- Interpretation: encoder/tokenization mismatch + few-shot anchoring.

Edge-case micro-examples (for summarization & constraint enforcement):
Input: Long changelog with nested bullets and code snippets.
Wanted output: 3 bullets, each <= 100 chars, and one 'backport_needed' boolean.
Shot A (good):
  IN: 'Fixed NPE in parser. Backported to 1.4 branch.'
  OUT: {"summary":"Fix NPE in parser","backport_needed":true}
Shot B (bad):
  IN: 'Refactor logging — affects formatting.'
  OUT: {"summary":"Refactor logging","backport_needed":false}
Stem: 'Produce JSON, 3 bullets at most, prefer present-tense short verbs.'

Notes on evaluation metrics for small tests:
- Prefer precision on structured fields (schema-level) over free-text ROUGE.
- Track 'schema-valid' (valid JSON + fields present) and 'semantic-match' (field-level intent).
- Keep a tiny seed of 40 examples (clean vs noisy) for regressions.

Open questions / TODOs (brain dump):
- Are we comfortable with 'assume non-sensitive' in demos? legal check w/ Maya.
- Should we have a canonical fallback token for citations? 'no-citation' vs empty list?
- Build a tiny harness that runs the 3 failure experiments above and produces a simple CSV of metrics. (Ticket: RL-3712)
- Try micro-calibration prompt: after generation, ask model to rate confidence 0–1 for each field. Does that correlate with correctness?

Quick reference snippets (copy-paste ready):
1) Output schema enforcement: "Return exactly JSON with keys: title:string OR null, bullets:array[string], error:null|string."
2) Minimal role anchor: "You are a terse assistant. Prioritize factual output over verbosity."
3) Typo robustness trick: "If text contains typos, normalize: correct obvious spellings but do not change named entities."

Random scratch notes (unresolved):
- When to prefer chain-of-thought vs direct answer for explainability in prod. My gut: CoT for dev-facing tools, not for user-facing low-latency endpoints.
- Add a 'contradiction detector' example to prompt library. Quick pattern: provide 2 supporting sentences + 1 contradictory; ask model to label contradiction index 0–2.

Session quick log:
2025-01-21 — ran 50-shot ablation with paraphrases, result: small improvements for L2 paraphrase but regressions when paraphrase density >50%.
2025-01-30 — knocked together a tiny JS harness to run 40 seed tests via hosted API; hooking up to console traces next.

Finish note: deliberately loose — the point is to capture practical, repeatable heuristics I can copy into demos or hand to someone on the team. If something here becomes stable, lift to conduit 'prompt-library' repo and make a proper test.

-- Ava M.
